en.title: Geography: the whole course
en.short: What geography is, how a geography degree is organised, the main areas, and how to study it.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text: Geography is the study of places, spaces and environments, and of how people and natural systems shape one another. It asks where things are, why they are there, how they connect across distance, and how those patterns change. Physical geography studies the atmosphere, water, landforms, soils and living systems. Human geography studies population, settlement, economy, culture, politics and development. Geography also has a strong technical side: maps, remote sensing, geographic information systems (GIS), statistics and fieldwork. These methods let geographers measure patterns and test explanations. It is both a natural and a social science, using evidence from field sites, censuses, satellite images and archives. It is not a list of capitals and products. The central habit is to link a pattern to a process and to a place.

sections.heading: How a degree is usually organised
sections.text: Degrees differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria, a BSc or BA in Geography is commonly a four-year full-time degree under National Universities Commission benchmark standards. Colleges of education award the NCE (Nigeria Certificate in Education) for geography teaching, and polytechnics offer related programmes such as surveying and geo-informatics under the National Board for Technical Education. In the United Kingdom, a BSc or BA usually takes three years full-time, four in Scotland, and some programmes add a placement or study-abroad year. In South Africa, a BSc is commonly three years, followed by an honours year before a master’s. Master’s awards are MSc or MA, often one year in the UK and longer in Nigeria; a PhD follows for research careers. Awards, course codes and entry requirements vary, so confirm them with your department.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Teaching moves from foundations to core courses and master’s work. Intro: the geographic perspective and Earth systems; maps, projections and map reading; Earth structure, rocks and plate tectonics; the atmosphere, weather and climate; geomorphic processes and landforms; soils, biogeography and ecosystems; population and settlement foundations; economic and cultural geography foundations; geographic data and descriptive statistics; and fieldwork and field observation.

Core: geomorphology and landscape evolution; climatology and climate change; hydrology and water resources; soil geography and land degradation; population geography and demography; urban geography and urbanisation; economic geography and globalisation; cultural and social geography; political geography and geopolitics; development geography and inequality; rural and agricultural geography; environmental hazards and resource management; GIS and spatial analysis; remote sensing and image interpretation; statistical methods for geography; and research methods and the field project.

Master’s: advanced geographical theory on space, place and landscape; advanced spatial analysis and GIScience; climate change adaptation and resilience; and research methods leading to a dissertation.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Study geography by connecting three things: a concept, a place and a method. For each topic, learn the key terms, draw the diagram or map, and find one real example. When you read about a process, ask what evidence would show it is happening and at what scale.

Practise map reading with scale, grid references, contours and symbols. Learn the distortions of common projections and when each is useful. Do the statistics by hand once, then with a spreadsheet or a GIS package. Keep a field notebook with dates, locations, sketches, photographs and notes on method. For climate and population data, record the source, year and definition.

Write short explanations from memory, then check them against your notes. Use past questions and mark schemes. Explain diagrams and cases to someone else.

sections.heading: Common mistakes students make
sections.text:
Students often memorise descriptions without explaining the process behind a pattern. They confuse weather with climate, and a landform with a landscape. They use a map without checking its scale, orientation, projection or date. They treat one case study as proof of a general rule.

In data work, the common errors are to ignore units, mix years or definitions, and treat correlation as causation. In fieldwork, poor records make the data unusable later. In essays, students sometimes list facts without an argument, or use outdated figures for climate, population or development.

Always state the scale and location you are discussing. Name the source and date of every statistic. Say clearly when something varies by country or over time. If two explanations are possible, set out both and say what evidence would decide between them.

keyPoints: Geography asks where things are, why they are there and how places connect.
Physical geography studies natural systems; human geography studies people, economies and societies.
Every map has scale, projection and purpose, so read it critically.
Link each concept to a place, a process and a method.
Record the source, date and definition of every statistic you use.
Degree length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook.

en.title: The Geographic Perspective and Earth Systems
en.short: Geography’s scope, spatial concepts, Earth’s four systems, human-environment relations, maps and models.

sections.heading: What geography studies
sections.text: Geography is the study of the Earth as the home of people. It asks where things are, why they are there, and what difference their location makes. Its scope runs from physical geography, which studies landforms, climate, water, soils and living things, to human geography, which studies population, settlement, economy, culture and politics. Geography joins the two, and uses maps, fieldwork and spatial data.

sections.heading: Spatial ideas
sections.text: Six spatial ideas organise geographical thinking. Location is where something is, either absolute (a grid reference) or relative (near a market). Place is a location given meaning by people. A region is an area sharing chosen features; regions are mental tools, not natural boxes. Scale is the size of the area studied, from a street to the globe. Distance is separation, measured in kilometres or in time and cost. Diffusion is the spread of an idea or thing through space, such as a crop variety passing from farm to farm.

sections.heading: Earth as systems
sections.text: Geographers treat the Earth as four interacting systems: the atmosphere (air), hydrosphere (water), lithosphere (rock and land) and biosphere (living things). A system is a set of parts linked by flows of energy and matter. Change in one part affects the others. A small case: Amina clears trees on a slope above her village. Less rain is intercepted, runoff increases, soil erodes into the stream, and the stream silts up. The lithosphere, biosphere and hydrosphere have all changed.

sections.heading: Human-environment and models
sections.text: Human-environment relations are studied without assuming that environment decides society (environmental determinism). The common view is possibilism: the environment sets limits and offers possibilities, and people choose among them. Geographers use maps and models because reality is too complex to hold at once. A model is a simplified representation of selected features or processes; a map is a model of space. Both are useful and both leave things out, so ask what was selected and why.

keyPoints: Geography studies spatial organisation and human-environment relations.
Location can be absolute or relative; place is location given meaning.
A region is a tool based on chosen features, not a fixed natural unit.
Earth works as four linked systems: atmosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and biosphere.
A change in one Earth system affects the others through flows of energy and matter.
Maps and models simplify reality, so always ask what they include and leave out.

en.title: Maps, Map Projections and Map Reading
en.short: Scale, latitude and longitude, projections and distortion, contours, symbols and thematic map design.

sections.heading: Scale and coordinates
sections.text:
Map scale is the ratio of map distance to ground distance. At 1:50,000, one unit on the map represents 50,000 of the same units on the ground. Two points 4 cm apart are 4 × 50,000 cm = 200,000 cm = 2 km apart. A bar scale stays usable when a map is enlarged or reduced; a representative fraction (a ratio) does not.

Latitude is angular distance north or south of the Equator, 0° to 90°. Longitude is angular distance east or west of the prime meridian, 0° to 180°. Projected maps also use grid coordinates, such as eastings and northings, read from the map grid.

sections.heading: Projections and distortion
sections.text: A map projection is a set of rules for transferring points from the curved Earth onto a flat sheet. This always distorts shape, area, distance or direction. Conformal projections preserve local angles and small shapes but exaggerate area away from the line where scale is true; Mercator is an example. Equal-area projections preserve area but distort shape. Equidistant projections preserve distance from one or two points or along certain lines. Compromise projections balance errors. No projection preserves all properties, so choose by purpose.

sections.heading: Topographic maps
sections.text: Topographic maps show relief and selected human and physical features at a large scale. The legend explains symbols for roads, rivers, buildings and vegetation. Contour lines join points of equal elevation. The contour interval is the height difference between neighbouring contours. Contours close together mean steep ground; widely spaced contours mean gentle ground. A contour crossing a valley points upstream. Spot heights and trigonometrical points give exact elevations.

sections.heading: Thematic maps
sections.text: Thematic maps show one theme, such as population density or rainfall. Choropleth maps shade administrative areas by value; proportional symbols vary symbol size; dot maps show counts. Cartographic communication depends on title, legend, scale, orientation, source and date. Colour and class breaks should suit the data and the reader. Maps are selective arguments, not neutral pictures, so read the legend and check what has been left out.

keyPoints: Scale = map distance ÷ ground distance, so ground distance = map distance × scale denominator.
At 1:50,000, 1 cm on the map represents 0.5 km on the ground.
Latitude gives north-south position from 0° to 90°; longitude gives east-west position from 0° to 180°.
Every projection distorts shape, area, distance or direction; conformal preserves shape and equal-area preserves area.
Contours join equal elevations; close spacing means steep slope and wide spacing means gentle slope.
Thematic maps communicate through title, legend, scale, source and suitable classification, and maps are selective.

en.title: Earth Structure, Rocks and Plate Tectonics
en.short: Earth’s layers, minerals and the rock cycle, plate boundaries, earthquakes and volcanoes.

sections.heading: Inside the Earth
sections.text:
The Earth is layered by density. The core is mostly iron and nickel; the inner core is solid, the outer core liquid, and its motion generates the magnetic field. Around it lies the mantle, solid rock that creeps very slowly.

The crust is continental (granite-like, thicker) or oceanic (basalt, denser). Crust plus upper mantle form the lithosphere, which rides on the softer asthenosphere.

sections.heading: Minerals and rocks
sections.text:
A mineral is a naturally occurring solid with a definite chemical composition and orderly atomic structure, such as quartz. Rocks are mixtures of minerals.

Igneous rock forms when magma or lava cools: slowly underground it is coarse-grained (granite), quickly at the surface fine-grained (basalt). Sedimentary rock forms from compacted sediment or dissolved material, such as limestone. Metamorphic rock forms when heat and pressure alter existing rock, as limestone becomes marble. The rock cycle links them: weathering makes sediment, burial and heat change it, melting returns it to magma.

sections.heading: Plate tectonics
sections.text:
Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912, citing matching coastlines and fossils; it was rejected until sea-floor spreading was shown in the 1960s. Plates move a few centimetres a year, driven by convection in the mantle and the pull of sinking plates.

At divergent boundaries plates separate and new crust forms, as at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. At convergent boundaries oceanic crust sinks (subduction), giving trenches and volcanic arcs, or continents collide and fold mountains rise. At transform boundaries plates slide past, causing shallow earthquakes.

sections.heading: Earthquakes and volcanoes
sections.text:
Earthquakes happen when stress in rock is released suddenly along a fault; the point of origin is the focus, and the point above it the epicentre. Seismic waves are recorded on seismographs.

Volcanoes form where magma reaches the surface, commonly at subduction zones, divergent boundaries or hot spots; a hot spot is a plume of hot rock that stays fixed while the plate moves over it. Their landforms include shield volcanoes (runny lava, gentle slopes) and steep composite cones (layered lava and ash).

keyPoints: The Earth has a core, mantle and crust, and the lithosphere rides on the asthenosphere.
A mineral has a definite composition and atomic structure; a rock is a mixture of minerals.
Igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks are linked by the rock cycle.
Divergent boundaries build new crust, convergent boundaries destroy or crumple it, transform boundaries slide.
Earthquake focus is underground; the epicentre is the point above it.
Volcano shape depends on lava type: runny lava gives shields, thick lava gives steep cones.

en.title: The Atmosphere, Weather and Climate
en.short: Covers atmospheric composition and layers, solar energy balance, weather variables, air masses and climate controls.

sections.heading: Composition and layers
sections.text: The atmosphere is a thin layer of gases held by gravity. Dry air is about 78 per cent nitrogen, 21 per cent oxygen and 1 per cent argon with other gases. Water vapour and carbon dioxide vary. Temperature defines the main layers. In the troposphere, where most weather occurs, temperature usually falls with height. In the stratosphere, ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation and temperature rises with height. Above are the mesosphere and thermosphere.

sections.heading: Energy balance
sections.text: Solar radiation arrives mainly as shortwave energy. The Earth absorbs some and reflects the rest; the reflected fraction is albedo. The surface warms and emits longwave infrared radiation. Greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit some longwave energy, keeping the surface warmer than it would otherwise be. At equilibrium, absorbed solar energy equals outgoing longwave energy. The surplus of solar energy near the equator and deficit near the poles drive winds and ocean currents.

sections.heading: Weather variables
sections.text:
Temperature falls with height at the environmental lapse rate, on average about 6.5 °C per kilometre in the troposphere. Pressure is the weight of air above a point, so it falls with height. Wind is air moving from high to low pressure; the Coriolis force deflects it right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern Hemisphere. Humidity is water vapour in air. Relative humidity compares actual vapour with the maximum possible at that temperature. Cooling to the dew point allows condensation and cloud; precipitation follows when droplets grow and fall.

Example: surface temperature 30 °C, lapse rate 6.5 °C per km. At 3 km: 30 − (6.5 × 3) = 30 − 19.5 = 10.5 °C. Real lapse rates vary.

sections.heading: Air masses and climate
sections.text: An air mass is a large body of air with similar temperature and humidity, named by source region, such as polar maritime. Fronts form where air masses meet. Climate controls include latitude, altitude, distance from the sea, ocean currents, prevailing winds, relief and vegetation. Coastal Lagos is humid; inland Kano is drier.

keyPoints: Dry air is about 78 per cent nitrogen and 21 per cent oxygen; water vapour varies.
The troposphere holds most weather and temperature usually falls with height there.
Albedo is the fraction of solar radiation reflected; at equilibrium absorbed solar equals outgoing longwave.
Wind flows from high to low pressure and is deflected by the Coriolis force.
Relative humidity is actual vapour divided by saturation vapour at the same temperature.
Temperature change with height is about −(lapse rate × height); at 6.5 °C per km, 3 km gives a fall of 19.5 °C.

en.title: Geomorphic Processes and Landforms
en.short: Weathering, mass movement, erosion, transport and deposition by rivers, ice, wind and waves, and resulting landforms.

sections.heading: Processes and terms
sections.text: Geomorphic processes change the shape of the land. Weathering is the breakdown of rock in place, by water, temperature change, plants or chemicals. It does not move the material. Mass movement is the downslope movement of soil and rock under gravity, from slow soil creep to fast landslides. Erosion is the removal of material by a moving agent such as water, ice, wind or waves. Transport carries it, and deposition drops it where the agent slows. These processes wear down high land and build new landforms elsewhere.

sections.heading: Rivers and slopes
sections.text: A river erodes by the force of water, by abrasion (sediment scraping the bed) and by solution (dissolving rock). It carries sediment as bed load (rolling grains), suspended load (fine grains in the water) and dissolved load. In the upper course, erosion cuts V-shaped valleys. Lower down, deposition builds floodplains (flat land beside the river) and deltas (sediment at the river mouth). A drainage basin is the area drained by a river and its tributaries; its boundary is the watershed or divide. On slopes, weathering produces regolith, loose broken rock. Creep moves it slowly downhill; a landslide is a faster slip.

sections.heading: Ice, wind and waves
sections.text: Glaciers erode by plucking (freezing onto rock and pulling it away) and abrasion (scraping). They deepen valleys into U-shapes and deposit moraines (piles of debris). Wind erodes by deflation (lifting loose grains) and by abrasion, sand-blasting rock. It deposits dunes where sand collects. Waves erode cliffs by water pressure and abrasion. Longshore drift moves sediment along the coast. Deposition builds beaches and spits (sand ridges reaching into the sea). Each agent leaves its own landforms.

sections.heading: Reading a landscape
sections.text: Imagine a steep Ethiopian hillside. Weathering makes regolith. Rain makes soil creep and landslides move material downslope. Streams carry the sediment through the drainage basin. On the plain, the river slows and deposits silt to build a floodplain. Landforms are not fixed: they change when climate, vegetation or land use changes the balance between erosion and deposition.

keyPoints: Weathering breaks rock in place, while erosion removes it and deposition lays it down.
Mass movement is gravity-driven downslope movement, from slow creep to fast landslides.
Rivers erode, transport and deposit sediment, making valleys, floodplains and deltas.
Glaciers, wind and waves each produce their own erosional and depositional landforms.
A drainage basin is bounded by a watershed, and slopes move regolith downhill.
Landforms change when the balance between erosion and deposition changes.

en.title: Soils, Biogeography and Ecosystems
en.short: Soil formation, profiles and properties, biomes, energy flow, nutrient cycles and human impacts.

sections.heading: Soil formation and profile
sections.text:
Soil is the weathered, organic-rich layer where roots grow. Five factors shape it: parent material, climate, organisms, relief and time. Climate and organisms act fastest; parent material supplies minerals; relief affects drainage; time allows horizons to form.

A soil profile is a vertical section. Typical horizons are O (litter), A (topsoil), B (subsoil), C (weathered rock) and R (bedrock). Properties include texture, structure, pH, organic matter, drainage and cation exchange capacity, which measures nutrient-holding ability.

sections.heading: Biomes and distributions
sections.text:
A biome is a regional community of plants and animals shaped by climate and soil. Major biomes include tropical rainforest, savanna, desert, temperate grassland, temperate forest, boreal forest and tundra. Latitude, rainfall, temperature and altitude control their distribution.

Plants and animals adapt to these conditions. Savanna grasses survive drought and fire, while acacia trees have deep roots. Desert succulents store water and many animals are nocturnal. Biogeography studies species distributions and dispersal.

sections.heading: Energy flow and nutrients
sections.text:
Energy enters most ecosystems as sunlight. Producers convert it by photosynthesis into food. Consumers eat producers or other consumers; decomposers break down dead matter. Energy is lost as heat at each trophic level, so food chains are short. A rough guide is ten per cent passing to the next level.

Carbon and nitrogen cycle through air, soil, water and organisms. Phosphorus cycles mainly through soil, water and organisms, as it has no significant gaseous phase. Decomposers release nutrients for reuse. If producers hold 10,000 units, 1,000 reach primary consumers, 100 secondary and 10 tertiary.

sections.heading: Human impacts
sections.text:
Farming, grazing, deforestation, irrigation, fertilisers, mining and urban growth change soils and ecosystems. Removing vegetation exposes soil to erosion by rain and wind. Overgrazing compacts soil and reduces cover. Irrigation can raise salinity. Fertilisers and pesticides can pollute water and harm biodiversity.

Responses include terracing, cover crops, manure, agroforestry and protected areas. In the Sahel, farmers use stone lines and manure to slow runoff and rebuild soil. Results depend on rainfall, land pressure and practice.

keyPoints: Soil forms through parent material, climate, organisms, relief and time.
A soil profile has horizons O, A, B, C and R; texture, structure, pH and cation exchange capacity are key properties.
A biome is a regional community shaped by climate and soil, and biogeography explains species distributions.
Energy flows one way through ecosystems and is lost as heat, so roughly ten per cent passes between trophic levels.
Nutrients such as carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus cycle and are reused by decomposers.
Human activities can cause erosion, salinity and biodiversity loss; terracing, cover crops and agroforestry reduce harm.

en.title: Population and Settlement Foundations
en.short: Population density, growth, pyramids, migration, and rural and urban settlement patterns.

sections.heading: Distribution and density
sections.text: Population distribution is how people are spread over an area. Density makes areas comparable: arithmetic density = total population ÷ land area. A district with 240,000 people in 3,000 km² has 240,000 ÷ 3,000 = 80 people per km². This average hides crowding and empty land. Physical factors such as relief, climate, water and soils, and human factors such as jobs and transport, help explain patterns. Density figures vary by country and area, so check the source.

sections.heading: Growth, pyramids and migration
sections.text: Population change has three components: births, deaths and migration. Natural increase = births − deaths. Net migration = immigrants − emigrants. Births 9,000, deaths 3,000, immigrants 1,500 and emigrants 500 give natural increase 6,000, net migration 1,000 and total growth 7,000. A population pyramid shows age and sex structure: a broad base suggests high birth rates, a narrow top fewer people reaching old age, often from shorter life expectancy. Migration can be voluntary or forced, internal or international; push factors drive people out and pull factors attract them.

sections.heading: Settlement patterns
sections.text: Settlements are places where people live and work. Rural settlements are often small and tied to farming; urban settlements are larger and denser. The boundary between them differs by country, so use the national definition. Common rural patterns are dispersed, with separate farmsteads, nucleated, with houses grouped around a centre, and linear, along a road, river or valley. Urban patterns include grid, radial and irregular layouts. Settlement growth can be planned or informal.

sections.heading: Site and situation
sections.text: Site is the actual ground a settlement occupies: a dry ridge, a river crossing or a sheltered harbour. Situation is its position relative to surrounding features such as routes, resources and other towns. Early sites often had water, fertile land, defence or trade advantages. A settlement may keep a good situation even when its site is poor. Site and situation are not permanent: new roads, ports or mines can change both.

keyPoints: Arithmetic density = total population ÷ land area; it is an average and can hide local crowding.
Population change = natural increase + net migration, where natural increase = births − deaths and net migration = immigrants − emigrants.
A population pyramid shows age and sex structure and hints at birth rates, life expectancy and migration.
Migration can be voluntary or forced, internal or international, and is shaped by push and pull factors.
Rural settlement patterns include dispersed, nucleated and linear; urban definitions vary by country.
Site is the actual ground of a settlement; situation is its position relative to routes, resources and other places.

en.title: Economic and Cultural Geography Foundations
en.short: Economic sectors, location and trade, culture regions and landscapes, and globalisation.

sections.heading: Economic sectors
sections.text: Economic activities are grouped into four sectors. Primary activities take raw materials from nature: farming, fishing, mining and forestry. Secondary activities process them: milling, refining, weaving and manufacturing. Tertiary activities provide services: transport, retail, banking, teaching and health care. Quaternary activities handle knowledge and decision-making: research, software, planning and administration. The sectors are linked; a cassava farmer (primary) supplies a mill (secondary), whose flour is sold by a trader (tertiary) and whose records are managed by an accountant (quaternary).

sections.heading: Location and trade
sections.text: Location factors make a place suitable for an activity. These include raw materials, energy, labour, transport, market, land, capital, government policy and agglomeration, the clustering of firms that share suppliers and workers. Trade lets places specialise. A country gains by producing goods where it has a lower opportunity cost, the next best option. Suppose a region can grow rice or cotton. If one hectare of rice earns 40,000 naira and cotton 30,000 naira, rice has the higher return; specialise in rice if cotton can be bought cheaply.

sections.heading: Culture and landscape
sections.text: Culture is a group’s learned way of life: beliefs, values, customs, language and technology. A culture region is an area where shared traits are common, though boundaries are gradual and overlapping. Language and religion mark regions. Ethnicity is a sense of identity based on ancestry, culture or history, not a fixed biological fact. Cultural landscapes are the visible results of people working on the land: fields, houses, markets, places of worship and monuments. A market town in Yorubaland, Nigeria, can show a mosque, church, palace and Yoruba street names.

sections.heading: Globalisation
sections.text: Globalisation is the growing movement of goods, money, people, information and ideas across borders. Cheaper transport, digital communication and trade rules drive it, and its effects are uneven. Some places gain jobs and technology; others face competition or lose control over local decisions. It spreads languages and products, but people adapt and resist, creating hybrid cultures.

keyPoints: Primary activities extract, secondary activities process, tertiary activities serve and quaternary activities handle knowledge.
Location factors include raw materials, labour, transport, market, agglomeration and government policy.
Trade allows specialisation according to opportunity cost, the next best option forgone.
A culture region is an area of shared traits with gradual, overlapping boundaries.
Ethnicity is a form of identity, not a fixed biological fact, and cultural landscapes show human work on the land.
Globalisation links places unevenly and can produce hybrid cultures rather than erasing local ones.

en.title: Geographic Data and Descriptive Statistics
en.short: Types and scales of geographic data, sources and sampling, summary statistics, graphs, rates and spatial displays.

sections.heading: Data types and scales
sections.text:
Geographic data describe places. Qualitative data are labels, such as land-use class; quantitative data are numbers, such as rainfall. Quantitative data are discrete when counted (schools) or continuous when measured (temperature). Spatial data are points (wells), lines (roads) or areas (districts).

Measurement scales: nominal = names with no order (soil type); ordinal = ranked but unequal gaps (low, medium, high risk); interval = equal units, no true zero (°C); ratio = equal units and true zero (mm), so ratios are meaningful.

sections.heading: Sources and sampling
sections.text:
Sources are primary, collected for your question (survey, measurement), or secondary, collected by others (census, records, satellite images). Check definitions, date and coverage.

A census counts everyone; a sample studies part. Random sampling gives every unit a known chance of selection. Systematic sampling takes every kth unit; stratified sampling samples within groups; cluster sampling selects whole groups. Sampling error is chance variation; bias is systematic distortion, such as surveying only town-centre residents.

sections.heading: Summarising data
sections.text:
A frequency distribution counts observations in each class or category. The mean is the sum divided by n. The median is the middle value when ordered; the mode is the most frequent. Dispersion measures spread: range = highest − lowest; standard deviation measures typical distance from the mean.

Example: 2, 4, 4, 6, 9. Mean = 25 ÷ 5 = 5. Median = 4. Mode = 4. Range = 9 − 2 = 7. Squared deviations: 9, 1, 1, 1, 16; sum = 28. Complete-set variance = 28 ÷ 5 = 5.6, standard deviation = √5.6 = 2.37. Sample variance = 28 ÷ 4 = 7, standard deviation = 2.65.

sections.heading: Graphs, rates and displays
sections.text:
Use bar charts for categories, histograms for grouped numbers, line graphs for time change and scatter plots for relationships. A rate compares one quantity with another, such as cases per 1,000 people. A ratio compares two quantities directly, such as 3:1. Percentages are proportions out of 100.

Spatial displays include dot maps, proportional symbols and choropleth maps. A choropleth shades areas by value; use rates or densities, not raw counts, or large areas look important only because they are large. Label units, source and year.

keyPoints: Nominal, ordinal, interval and ratio scales differ in order and true zero; ratio data allow meaningful ratios.
Primary data are collected for your question; secondary data were collected by others and need checking for definitions, date and coverage.
Random sampling gives every unit a known chance of selection; bias is systematic, while sampling error is chance variation.
Mean = Σx ÷ n; median = middle ordered value; mode = most frequent value.
Range = highest − lowest; standard deviation = √(Σ(x − mean)² ÷ n) for a complete set, or ÷ (n − 1) for a sample.
Use rates or densities in choropleth maps, not raw counts, and label units, source and year.

en.title: Fieldwork and Field Observation
en.short: Purposes, design, instruments, recording, sketch maps, transects, safety, ethics and field reports.

sections.heading: Why fieldwork
sections.text: Fieldwork means going to a place to collect first-hand information. It trains observation, tests ideas against real conditions, and builds skill in measuring and recording. A study starts with a clear question. For example, a student may ask how stall density changes across a market in Kano. The question decides the site, variables and number of observations. Without it, notes become unrelated facts.

sections.heading: Design and instruments
sections.text:
Design means choosing what to observe, where, when and how often. Define each variable and its unit before going out. Use a sampling plan: random points, a grid, or fixed intervals along a line. Take repeat readings and record conditions that may affect them, such as time of day or weather.

Instruments depend on the task. A tape measures distance, a compass gives direction, a clinometer estimates slope angle, and a GPS records position. Check instruments before leaving and carry spares.

sections.heading: Recording and maps
sections.text: Record in a field notebook with date, time, place, observer, weather, units and method. Write numbers clearly and note anything unusual. Photographs and labelled sketches support the notes. Never rely on memory. A sketch map is a simple plan view with a scale, north arrow, key and labels. A transect is a line across a site; record what occurs at intervals along it, such as soil, plants or land use.

sections.heading: Safety, ethics, report
sections.text: Before fieldwork, assess risks and tell someone your route and return time. Work in pairs, get permission to enter land, respect local customs, and avoid unsafe ground or water. Ethics means informed consent, privacy, honesty and no harm to people or sites. A simple field report gives title, aim, location, methods, results, discussion, limitations and conclusion. It should show enough detail for another student to repeat the work.

keyPoints: Fieldwork collects first-hand data to describe patterns, test ideas and build practical skill.
A clear question decides the site, variables, sampling plan and number of observations.
Define variables and units, take repeat readings and record conditions that affect measurement.
A field notebook records date, time, place, observer, weather, units and method; sketches and photographs support it.
A sketch map needs a scale, north arrow, key and labels; a transect records changes along a line.
Safety and ethics require risk assessment, permission, consent, privacy and honesty; a field report states aim, methods, results, limitations and conclusion.

en.title: Geomorphology and Landscape Evolution
en.short: Geomorphic systems, slopes, rivers, ice, coasts, deserts, Quaternary change and applied geomorphology.

sections.heading: Systems and equilibrium
sections.text: A geomorphic system links landforms and processes by flows of energy and matter. Equilibrium means the landform adjusts to those flows; dynamic equilibrium means adjustment continues around a stable average. A threshold is a condition that must be crossed before the system changes abruptly, such as a slope becoming unstable after heavy rain. A sediment budget compares input, output and storage: input − output = change in storage. In a catchment, input 1,200 tonnes a year and output 800 tonnes a year give storage growth of 400 tonnes a year. A trap holding 2,000 tonnes fills in 2,000 ÷ 400 = 5 years.

sections.heading: Slopes and rivers
sections.text: On slopes, weathering breaks rock, and mass movement moves soil and rock downslope under gravity, helped or hindered by water. Creep is slow; landslides are fast. Rivers erode, transport and deposit sediment. They cut down toward base level, the lowest level to which they can erode, and build floodplains and terraces when sediment supply or sea level changes.

sections.heading: Ice, coasts and deserts
sections.text: Glaciers erode by scraping and pulling rock away, and deposit debris; their valleys are often U-shaped. Coasts are shaped by waves, tides and sediment supply, producing beaches and cliffs. In arid environments, rare but intense rain and wind move sediment, forming dunes and flash-flood channels.

sections.heading: Long-term change and use
sections.text: Over millions of years, tectonics and climate control uplift, erosion, sediment deposition and river downcutting. The Quaternary, the last about 2.6 million years, saw repeated glacial and interglacial cycles that left terraces, wind-blown silt and altered coastlines. Applied geomorphology uses these ideas in land-use planning and hazard assessment, for example mapping landslide risk before building.

keyPoints: A geomorphic system links landforms and processes through flows of energy and matter.
Equilibrium is adjustment to those flows; a threshold is a condition that causes abrupt change.
Sediment budget: input − output = change in storage.
Slope factor of safety = resisting forces ÷ driving forces; values below 1 suggest failure is likely.
Rivers, glaciers, coasts and arid processes erode, transport and deposit sediment, leaving distinctive landforms.
Quaternary glacial cycles and tectonics shape long-term landscapes; geomorphology informs land-use planning and hazard assessment.

en.title: Climatology and Climate Change
en.short: Circulation, climate classification, ENSO, variability, evidence, causes, impacts, adaptation and mitigation.

sections.heading: Circulation and classification
sections.text: Global circulation moves heat from the tropics poleward. Hadley cells lift moist air near the equator, forming the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) and heavy rain, and descend dry air near 30°, where most deserts lie. Ferrel and polar cells complete the pattern. Trade winds, westerlies and jet streams steer weather systems. Climate classification groups places by long-term temperature and rainfall. The Köppen system uses monthly temperature and precipitation thresholds and vegetation; Thornthwaite uses moisture and thermal efficiency. Classifications are useful summaries, not explanations, and boundaries shift as data improve.

sections.heading: Ocean and variability
sections.text: Ocean and atmosphere exchange heat, water and momentum. In the tropical Pacific, the Walker circulation normally piles warm water west and upwells cold water east. During El Niño, weakened trade winds let warm water spread east, altering rainfall worldwide through teleconnections, links between distant climate events; La Niña is the cool phase. Together these swings are the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO). The Indian Ocean Dipole and North Atlantic Oscillation are other modes. Climate variability is fluctuation around a mean; climate change is a sustained shift in that mean or its variability. A single season cannot prove either.

sections.heading: Evidence and causes
sections.text: Evidence comes from instrumental records, ice cores, tree rings, corals and sediments. They show past CO2 and temperature changes and a warming trend since the industrial era. Causes include greenhouse gases, aerosols, volcanic dust, solar variation and orbital cycles (Milankovitch). Greenhouse gases trap outgoing infrared radiation; human emissions have raised their concentration. The IPCC synthesises peer-reviewed evidence. Scientists attribute most recent warming to human activity; natural factors alone do not explain it.

sections.heading: Impacts and responses
sections.text: Impacts include heatwaves, shifting rainfall, droughts, floods, sea-level rise and risks to food and water. Vulnerability depends on exposure, sensitivity and adaptive capacity. Adaptation reduces harm: early warning, drainage, drought-resistant crops, water harvesting. Mitigation reduces emissions: renewable energy, efficiency, forest protection. In Lagos, Nigeria, coastal flooding may be met with drainage and planning (adaptation), while cleaner transport cuts emissions (mitigation). Poorer groups often adapt least, so finance and equity matter.

keyPoints: Hadley, Ferrel and polar cells and the ITCZ explain broad belts of rain and desert.
Köppen and Thornthwaite classify climate from long-term temperature and moisture data.
El Niño and La Niña are phases of ENSO that shift Pacific winds, upwelling and rainfall worldwide.
Climate variability is short-term fluctuation; climate change is a sustained shift.
Evidence for climate change comes from instrumental and proxy records; greenhouse gases are the main human cause of recent warming.
Adaptation reduces climate harm; mitigation reduces greenhouse gas emissions.

en.title: Hydrology and Water Resources
en.short: The water cycle, catchment processes, water balance, hydrographs, groundwater, quality, scarcity and water conflict.

sections.heading: Catchment processes
sections.text: A catchment is the area drained by a river and its tributaries, bounded by a divide. The hydrological cycle moves water as vapour, liquid and ice between ocean, atmosphere and land. In a catchment, precipitation is the main input. Evaporation from surfaces and transpiration from plants, together called evapotranspiration, return water to the air. Some water infiltrates soil and recharges groundwater, some flows overland as runoff, and some is stored in soil, lakes, snow or aquifers. These vary with climate, geology, soils, vegetation and land use.

sections.heading: Water balance
sections.text: The water balance for a catchment over a period is P = ET + Q + ΔS, where P is precipitation, ET evapotranspiration, Q streamflow (runoff) and ΔS change in storage; all in millimetres over the same period. If P = 1200 mm, ET = 700 mm and Q = 350 mm, then ΔS = 1200 − 700 − 350 = 150 mm. The runoff coefficient is Q ÷ P = 350 ÷ 1200 = 0.29, so 29 per cent of rainfall became streamflow. Check: 700 + 350 + 150 = 1200 mm.

sections.heading: Hydrographs
sections.text: A storm hydrograph plots river discharge against time. It has a rising limb, peak and recession limb. Lag time is the delay between peak rainfall and peak discharge. Steep, flashy hydrographs follow impermeable soils, steep slopes, urban surfaces or little vegetation. Gentle hydrographs follow permeable ground, gentle slopes, forest or groundwater stores. Baseflow is the groundwater contribution between storms.

sections.heading: Quality and conflict
sections.text: Water quality describes chemical, physical and biological suitability for uses such as drinking, irrigation and ecosystems. Pollution from sewage, fertiliser, mining or industry can make water unsafe. Water scarcity can be physical, where demand exceeds supply, or economic, where supply exists but money or institutions are lacking. Management uses catchment planning, dams, groundwater rules, pricing and pollution control. Transboundary basins can create conflict over allocation, but also cooperation through treaties and basin authorities. Rules differ by country, so check official sources.

keyPoints: A catchment is the area drained by a river and its tributaries, bounded by a divide.
The catchment water balance is P = ET + Q + ΔS, with all terms in the same units and period.
Runoff coefficient = Q ÷ P; in the example 350 ÷ 1200 = 0.29.
A hydrograph plots discharge against time; lag time separates peak rainfall from peak discharge.
Physical scarcity means demand exceeds supply; economic scarcity means institutions or money are lacking.
Transboundary water allocation can cause conflict and cooperation; rules differ by country, so check official sources.

en.title: Soil Geography and Land Degradation
en.short: Soil classification, fertility, erosion, salinisation, desertification and sustainable land management.

sections.heading: Classifying and mapping soils
sections.text: Soil classification groups soils by measurable properties and by the horizons of their profiles. A horizon is a layer parallel to the surface; a diagnostic horizon is one used to define a class. Two common international systems are the World Reference Base for Soil Resources and USDA Soil Taxonomy. Soil mapping is a survey that divides land into map units with similar soils, shown at a stated scale. GIS helps store and overlay these units. Local names and national systems vary, so state the system used.

sections.heading: Soil fertility and plants
sections.text: Soil fertility is the capacity of a soil to supply nutrients in forms plants can take up. Cation exchange capacity (CEC) is the number of negatively charged sites holding cations such as calcium, magnesium and potassium. Base saturation is the share of CEC occupied by base cations. If CEC is 12 cmol(+)/kg and exchangeable calcium, magnesium and potassium total 8 + 3 + 0.5 = 11.5 cmol(+)/kg, base saturation is (11.5 ÷ 12) × 100 = 95.8 per cent. High base saturation favours fertility, but pH, organic matter, water and rooting depth also matter.

sections.heading: Land degradation
sections.text: Land degradation is a decline in the land’s capacity to support plants and people. Water erosion removes soil by splash, sheet, rill and gully flow; wind erosion blows away dry, bare soil. Salinisation is the build-up of soluble salts, often from irrigation without drainage. Sodicity is a high share of sodium on the exchange complex, which damages structure. Desertification is land degradation in drylands; it is not the advance of desert dunes. Compaction and nutrient depletion are other forms.

sections.heading: Conservation and management
sections.text: Sustainable land management uses practices that keep soil productive without damaging it. Examples are contour ploughing, terracing, cover crops, agroforestry, reduced tillage, drainage and gypsum for sodic soils. In a dryland case, a farmer on a slope can combine contour bunds with crop rotation and manure. This slows runoff, adds organic matter and spreads risk. Practices must fit local soils.

keyPoints: Soil classification uses diagnostic horizons and measurable properties; the World Reference Base and USDA Soil Taxonomy are common systems.
Soil maps divide land into map units at a stated scale, and GIS helps overlay them.
CEC measures exchangeable cations, and base saturation = (sum of base cations ÷ CEC) × 100.
Water and wind erosion, salinisation, sodicity, compaction and nutrient depletion are major degradation forms.
Desertification is land degradation in drylands, not simply the advance of desert dunes.
Sustainable land management fits practices such as terracing, cover crops, agroforestry and drainage to local soils and rainfall.

en.title: Population Geography and Demography
en.short: It covers the demographic transition, fertility, mortality and migration theories, ageing, policy and census limits.

sections.heading: Transition and theory
sections.text: The demographic transition is the long shift from high birth and death rates to low ones. In the classic model, mortality falls first, fertility follows later, and population growth is fastest in between. The model is a description, not a law: timing and paths vary by country, and some states have stalled or reversed. Fertility means births; mortality means deaths. Fertility theories explain birth decline through economic change, child survival, education, urban life, and the spread of new ideas. Mortality theories include the epidemiological transition, in which infectious disease gives way to chronic disease, though not everywhere. Migration theories include push-pull, neoclassical wage differences, the new economics of labour migration, and network theory.

sections.heading: Structure and ageing
sections.text: A population pyramid shows age and sex structure. The dependency ratio compares dependants, usually people under 15 and over 64, with the working-age population. Ageing raises old-age dependency and can strain pensions and health care. A demographic dividend can occur when the working-age share rises, but only with jobs and education.

sections.heading: Data and policy
sections.text: A census counts a whole population at one time. It is limited by undercount, missing people, unclear definitions, recall error and incomplete vital registration, the official recording of births and deaths. Population policies may be pronatalist, antinatalist, or migration-based. They raise ethical questions about coercion and rights.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
Take a population of 1,000: 300 aged 0-14, 600 aged 15-64, and 100 aged 65+.
Youth dependency = 300 ÷ 600 × 100 = 50.
Old-age dependency = 100 ÷ 600 × 100 = 16.7.
Total dependency = 400 ÷ 600 × 100 = 66.7.
This means there are about 67 dependants per 100 working-age people.

keyPoints: The demographic transition describes a long shift from high to low birth and death rates, with the fastest growth in between.
Fertility, mortality and migration theories explain different parts of population change and should be used together.
A population pyramid shows age and sex structure; ageing raises old-age dependency.
Dependency ratio = dependants ÷ working-age population × 100.
Census data are limited by undercount, definition differences, recall error and incomplete vital registration.
Population policies may be pronatalist, antinatalist or migration-based, and raise ethical questions.

en.title: Urban Geography and Urbanisation
en.short: Urban growth and systems, land use models, housing, transport, informal settlements, planning and sustainable cities.

sections.heading: Growth and urban systems
sections.text:
Urbanisation is the rising share of a population living in towns and cities. Urban growth is the absolute rise in urban population. A country’s cities form an urban system: towns and cities linked by migration, trade, transport and services.

The rank-size rule says the nth largest city is roughly 1/n the size of the largest. A primate city is far larger than the next cities. Central place theory explains settlements as centres supplying goods and services to surrounding areas.

sections.heading: Land use and structure
sections.text:
Land use models describe how activities are arranged in cities. The concentric zone model (Burgess) has rings around a central business district. The sector model (Hoyt) has wedges along transport routes. The multiple nuclei model (Harris and Ullman) has several centres.

These models came from Western cities and are guides, not laws. Many African cities combine a colonial core, planned suburbs, informal settlements and expanding peri-urban areas, where city and countryside mix.

sections.heading: Housing, transport, informality
sections.text:
Housing is shaped by land prices, tenure and income. Transport links homes to work, schools and markets; poor transport raises costs and limits access. Informal settlements are areas where residents lack secure tenure and reliable basic services. They are not simply chaotic: residents build, rent and organise.

Consider Amina, who lives in an informal settlement beside a West African city. A new bus rapid transit line could shorten her journey, but without secure tenure and affordable fares she may be displaced or priced out. Planning must link transport, housing and land rights.

sections.heading: Planning and sustainable cities
sections.text:
Urban planning guides land use, infrastructure and public space. Urban governance is how governments, residents and firms make and enforce decisions. Sustainable cities aim to meet present needs without shifting costs to future residents or ecosystems.

Common goals include compact growth, public transport, serviced land, green space and participation. Progress depends on finance, capacity and secure land rights. A plan that ignores informal workers or tenants is unlikely to work.

keyPoints: Urbanisation is the rising urban share of a population; urban growth is the absolute increase in urban population.
Cities form systems linked by migration, trade and transport, and the rank-size rule gives the nth city as roughly largest city ÷ n.
Concentric zone, sector and multiple nuclei models are useful guides but were built from Western cities and do not fit every city.
Informal settlements are defined by insecure tenure and inadequate services, not by disorder.
Transport, housing and land rights must be planned together, or improvements can displace poor residents.
Sustainable urban planning needs finance, state capacity, participation and secure land rights.

en.title: Economic Geography and Globalisation
en.short: Location theory, agglomeration, global production networks and uneven development under globalisation.

sections.heading: Location and distance
sections.text:
Location theory explains where firms choose to produce. Weber’s least-cost model weighs transport and labour costs. Weight-losing industries, using bulky local inputs, tend to locate near materials; weight-gaining industries tend to locate near markets. Service firms depend more on market potential and access, as central place theory shows.

Worked example: input 4 tonnes from S, product 2 tonnes at M, transport 2 per tonne-km. At X (10 km from S, 20 km from M): (4 × 10 × 2) + (2 × 20 × 2) = 80 + 80 = 160. At Y (25 km from S, 8 km from M): (4 × 25 × 2) + (2 × 8 × 2) = 200 + 32 = 232. X is cheaper by 72, but labour or agglomeration savings can change the choice.

sections.heading: Agglomeration and regions
sections.text:
Agglomeration is the clustering of firms and workers. It lowers costs through shared suppliers, a larger labour pool and knowledge spillovers, as Marshall noted. Congestion and high rents can cause deglomeration.

Regional inequality often follows a core-periphery pattern: growth concentrates in core regions, while peripheral regions may lose skilled workers and investment. Myrdal’s cumulative causation describes this self-reinforcing process; spread effects can diffuse growth, but backwash effects may dominate.

sections.heading: Production networks and trade
sections.text:
Global production networks (GPNs) are cross-border arrangements in which firms, states and suppliers organise design, production and distribution. Global value chains describe the sequence of activities and who captures value.

Comparative advantage says specialisation raises total output when opportunity costs differ. Intra-industry trade and economies of scale also matter. Tariffs, transport costs and rules of origin shape where activities locate.

sections.heading: Uneven development
sections.text:
Globalisation integrates markets but does not make development even. Foreign investment and jobs may concentrate in regions with ports, skills and infrastructure, while others remain marginal.

Special economic zones can attract export work, but gains depend on linkages, wages and labour conditions. Uneven development is therefore a geographical outcome of location choices, agglomeration and power in production networks, not a single process.

keyPoints: Location theory weighs transport, labour and market access; least-cost sites minimise total cost.
Transport cost = weight × distance × rate, summed for inputs and products.
Agglomeration lowers costs through shared suppliers, labour pools and knowledge spillovers, but congestion can reverse it.
Core-periphery and cumulative causation help explain persistent regional inequality.
Global production networks and value chains show that trade and production are organised across borders, with value captured unevenly.
Globalisation produces uneven development because investment and jobs concentrate where infrastructure, skills and linkages are strong.

en.title: Cultural and Social Geography: Place, Identity and Difference
en.short: Place, identity, cultural landscapes, language, religion, ethnicity, gender, migration, diaspora and spatial exclusion.

sections.heading: Place, identity and landscape
sections.text:
Place is a location given meaning by people; identity is how people see themselves and are seen by others. Yi-Fu Tuan and Edward Relph showed that attachment to place, or its loss, shapes belonging. A sense of place can be strengthened by shared memory and weakened by displacement.

A cultural landscape is the visible result of people living in and changing an environment. Carl Sauer’s Berkeley school read landscapes as records of culture, but later geographers stress that landscapes are contested and change with power.

sections.heading: Language, religion and ethnicity
sections.text: Language, religion and ethnicity mark social groups and often mark territory. Language can unite a community or exclude outsiders, especially where school or official languages differ from home languages. Religion shapes sacred sites, calendars and everyday routines. Ethnicity is not simply inherited; it is a social construction that people use to draw boundaries. These identities overlap and can be used politically.

sections.heading: Gender, migration and diaspora
sections.text: Gender shapes migration and settlement. Women and men often move for different reasons and find different work, and migration can change household roles. A diaspora is a group living away from a homeland while keeping links to it. Diasporas build places of worship, shops and media, and send remittances. They also face questions of belonging in host societies.

sections.heading: Social difference and exclusion
sections.text: Social difference becomes spatial exclusion when groups are kept apart by distance, barriers, policing or law. South Africa’s apartheid Group Areas Act (1950) divided urban space by race; District Six in Cape Town was declared a white area and its community displaced. Such cases show that space is not neutral: it reflects and reproduces inequality. Spatial exclusion can be measured by access to services, transport and public space. Intersectionality reminds us that class, race, gender and migration status can combine.

keyPoints: Place is a location given meaning, and identity is how people see themselves and are seen by others.
Cultural landscapes are visible and contested records of human activity.
Language, religion and ethnicity draw social boundaries and can be used politically.
Migration is gendered, and diasporas keep links with a homeland while building new places.
Spatial exclusion keeps groups apart through distance, barriers, policing or law.
South Africa’s apartheid Group Areas Act (1950) is a clear case of law producing spatial exclusion.

en.title: Political Geography and Geopolitics
en.short: Territory, sovereignty, boundaries, geopolitics, electoral geography, nationalism and resource politics.

sections.heading: Territory and sovereignty
sections.text: A state is a political unit with population, territory, government and capacity to act internationally. Sovereignty is its supreme authority inside that territory and formal independence outside. Territory is not just a container: land, sea, airspace and resources are claimed and disputed. In the Bakassi peninsula case, Nigeria and Cameroon disputed territory; the International Court of Justice ruled for Cameroon in 2002, and Nigeria transferred the area in 2008. Legal title, colonial treaties and politics all shaped the outcome.

sections.heading: Boundaries and borderlands
sections.text: Boundaries are lines separating jurisdictions; borderlands are the zones people inhabit and cross. A boundary may follow a river, watershed or latitude. Border studies shows how checkpoints, documents and trade make borders real in daily life. In Africa, the Organisation of African Unity’s 1964 Cairo resolution urged states to respect borders inherited at independence, to reduce conflict, even where those borders split communities.

sections.heading: Classical and critical geopolitics
sections.text: Geopolitics studies how geography shapes political power and how actors use geographical ideas. Classical geopolitics, such as Halford Mackinder’s 1904 heartland thesis, treated control of strategic space as the key to power. Critics say it naturalises rivalry. Critical geopolitics examines how maps, speeches and news represent places as threats or opportunities, and how those representations justify policy. It asks who draws the line and for whose benefit.

sections.heading: Elections, nationalism and resources
sections.text: Electoral geography studies spatial voting patterns and constituency design. Malapportionment gives districts unequal voter numbers; gerrymandering draws boundaries to favour a party. Nationalism ties a people to a claimed homeland and may be civic or ethnic, though the line blurs. Resource politics concerns control of oil, minerals, water or land and the sharing of revenues. Abundant resources can fund conflict or weak institutions, often called the resource curse, but outcomes vary with institutions and prices.

keyPoints: Statehood usually requires population, territory, government and capacity to act internationally, while sovereignty is supreme authority within and independence outside.
Boundaries are legal lines; borderlands are lived zones where trade and kinship cross.
Classical geopolitics treats strategic space as power; critical geopolitics studies representations that justify policy.
Electoral geography links voting to place through malapportionment and gerrymandering.
Nationalism claims a homeland for a people and can be civic or ethnic.
Resource politics asks who controls and benefits from resources; abundance can fund conflict, but outcomes vary with institutions and prices.

en.title: Development Geography and Inequality
en.short: Colonial roots, development measures, rural livelihoods, aid and trade, the SDGs and regional inequality.

sections.heading: Colonial roots
sections.text: Colonial economies often exported one or two primary commodities, with railways and ports serving extraction rather than local markets. After independence, many states inherited weak industry, unequal land access and borders drawn for imperial convenience. Dependency theory argues that poor countries remain suppliers of cheap raw materials and buyers of costly manufactures, so trade gains are uneven. Others stress domestic institutions, conflict and policy. Postcolonial development means inherited structures plus post-independence choices.

sections.heading: Measuring development
sections.text: Development is wider than income. Gross domestic product (GDP) per person measures output, not health or education. The Human Development Index (HDI) combines life expectancy, schooling and gross national income (GNI) per person, adjusted for purchasing power parity (PPP), which compares local buying power. National poverty lines differ by country, and the World Bank also uses an international poverty line, updated over time. The Gini coefficient measures inequality from 0 (equal) to 1 (unequal). Example: incomes 1, 2, 3, 4, 10 have mean 4 and Gini 0.4, a high Gini despite a modest mean.

sections.heading: Livelihoods, aid, trade
sections.text: Rural livelihoods depend on assets: natural, human, financial, social and physical. Poor households reduce risk by diversifying income and sharing labour and food. Aid can fund schools, health and infrastructure, but it may be tied to donors’ suppliers or carry conditions. Trade can raise incomes, yet tariffs, subsidies and rules of origin can block poor producers. Fair trade and regional agreements aim at fairer exchange. Evidence on aid and trade is mixed, so avoid simple claims.

sections.heading: SDGs and regions
sections.text: The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), adopted by the United Nations in 2015 with a 2030 target, set 17 goals linking poverty, health, education, inequality, environment and partnerships. They are voluntary and indicator-based, so progress varies. Regional disparities appear within countries as well as between them: coastal and urban regions often attract investment while remote rural areas lack roads, clinics and markets. Geography matters through location, climate and access. Policy must combine national and place-based action.

keyPoints: Colonial export economies and unequal land access shape postcolonial development, though domestic institutions and policy also matter.
GDP per person measures output only; HDI adds life expectancy, schooling and GNI per person in PPP terms.
National poverty lines differ by country, so compare them only with care.
Gini coefficient: G = ΣΣ|xi − xj| ÷ (2n²μ), where μ is mean income and n is population size.
Rural livelihoods rest on natural, human, financial, social and physical assets, and poor households often diversify to reduce risk.
The SDGs are voluntary UN goals for 2030; aid and trade effects are mixed, and regional disparities need place-based policy.

en.title: Rural and Agricultural Geography
en.short: Covers farming systems, von Thünen location, land tenure, food security, irrigation and pastoralism.

sections.heading: Farming systems
sections.text: An agricultural system is the set of crops, livestock, tools, labour and land practices a farm or region uses. Systems are classified by purpose (subsistence or commercial), intensity (intensive or extensive), water source (rainfed or irrigated) and mobility (sedentary or pastoral). Shifting cultivation, wet-rice farming, mixed farming, plantations and nomadic pastoralism are standard types. Each reflects climate, soil, population density, market access and culture.

sections.heading: Location and rent
sections.text:
Von Thünen’s 1826 model explains location. Assume a uniform plain, one market, transport costs rising with distance, and farmers choosing the crop that pays the highest land rent. Rent equals revenue minus production cost minus transport cost. Perishable or bulky goods locate near the market.

Example: price 100 per tonne, yield 5 tonnes per hectare, production cost 300 per hectare, transport 2 per tonne per km. At 10 km: rent = (100 × 5) − 300 − (2 × 10 × 5) = 500 − 300 − 100 = 100 per hectare. At 20 km transport is 200, so rent is zero. The model is simple but still teaches distance decay.

sections.heading: Tenure and change
sections.text: Land tenure is the set of rules governing who may use, transfer or inherit land. Common forms are customary or communal tenure, private freehold, leasehold and state ownership. Security of tenure encourages investment, but insecure or gendered rights can weaken it. Agrarian change includes commercialisation, mechanisation, the Green Revolution, land reform and rural migration. Some of these changes can raise output, but they can also widen inequality and landlessness.

sections.heading: Food, water and development
sections.text: Food security means reliable access to sufficient, safe, nutritious food; it has four dimensions: availability, access, utilisation and stability. Rural livelihoods depend on natural, physical, human, financial and social assets, and on vulnerability to drought, prices and conflict. Irrigation can raise yields, but poor drainage causes waterlogging and salinisation. Pastoralism uses mobility and common grazing to manage drylands; transhumance is seasonal movement. Rural development works better when it combines infrastructure, credit, extension services, market access and local institutions.

keyPoints: Agricultural systems are classified by purpose, intensity, water source and mobility.
Von Thünen’s model locates land uses by distance to market and transport cost.
Land rent = revenue − production cost − transport cost.
Land tenure rules shape investment, equity and agrarian change.
Food security requires availability, access, utilisation and stability.
Irrigation and pastoralism need careful water and grazing management to avoid degradation.

en.title: Environmental Hazards and Resource Management
en.short: Hazard, risk and vulnerability, disaster cycle, resource conservation, EIA and community management.

sections.heading: Hazard, risk, vulnerability
sections.text:
A hazard is a potential source of harm: a flood, earthquake, drought, landslide or industrial spill. Hazards may be natural, technological or social. Risk is the chance of harmful consequences when a hazard meets exposed people or assets. Vulnerability is the conditions that make harm more likely or severe, such as poverty, poor housing or unsafe location. Exposure is being in a hazardous place; capacity is the ability to cope and recover. Risk rises with hazard, exposure and vulnerability, and falls with capacity.

A disaster occurs when a hazard overwhelms local capacity. The same flood may be a disaster in one settlement and a nuisance in another.

sections.heading: Disaster cycle
sections.text: The disaster cycle is a planning model, not a fixed sequence. Mitigation reduces hazard or vulnerability before an event. Preparedness includes early warning, drills, stocks and evacuation plans. Response saves lives during and after an event: rescue, shelter, water and health care. Recovery repairs services and livelihoods; reconstruction rebuilds assets. Recovery can reduce future risk. Phases often overlap.

sections.heading: Resources and conservation
sections.text: Resources are things people value and use, such as land, water and minerals. Renewable resources regenerate if use stays within their renewal rate; non-renewable resources are finite. Conservation means using resources wisely for present and future users. It includes reducing waste, recycling, efficiency and protecting habitats. Sustainable development meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. Common-pool resources need agreed rules and monitoring; community management works where users share information and enforce rules.

sections.heading: EIA and community management
sections.text:
Environmental impact assessment (EIA) predicts a project’s likely environmental and social effects before approval. Steps include screening, scoping, baseline study, impact prediction, mitigation, public review, decision and monitoring. Rules differ by country; check current national law. Community-based management involves local people in planning, using and monitoring resources. It combines local knowledge with technical advice but needs clear rights, fair benefits and support.

Case: a quarry near a river. Amina maps water sources; the EIA adds dust impacts; buffer zones and monitoring follow.

keyPoints: A hazard is a potential source of harm; risk is the chance of harm when hazard, exposure and vulnerability meet.
Vulnerability explains why the same hazard causes different losses in different places.
The disaster cycle links mitigation, preparedness, response, recovery and reconstruction; phases often overlap.
Conservation and sustainable development aim to keep resource use within renewal rates and protect future options.
EIA predicts environmental and social effects before approval and should include public review and monitoring.
Community-based management can improve local resource decisions but needs clear rights, fair benefits and support.

en.title: GIS and Spatial Analysis
en.short: Vector and raster data, georeferencing, overlay, buffering, terrain, interpolation and limits of GIS.

sections.heading: Data models and georeferencing
sections.text: A geographic information system (GIS) stores locations, attributes and relationships, then answers spatial questions. Vector data represent features as points, lines and polygons. Raster data divide space into a grid of cells, each holding one value. Georeferencing ties the data to real coordinates using control points and a transformation; without it, layers cannot be compared. A spatial database holds geometry, attributes and topology, which records neighbours and connections, so queries can combine location with tabular conditions.

sections.heading: Overlay, buffers and terrain
sections.text: Overlay combines layers. Vector overlay uses geometry: clip, intersect and union. Raster overlay works cell by cell. A buffer is a zone within a set distance of a feature. Terrain analysis uses a digital elevation model (DEM), a raster of elevations, to derive slope, aspect, hillshade and catchments. Worked example: two raster layers cover 200 × 200 cells at 10 m resolution. Each cell is 100 m², so the area is 4 km². If layer A marks 30% of cells and layer B marks 40%, an intersect of independent layers has about 0.30 × 0.40 × 40,000 = 4,800 cells, or 0.48 km².

sections.heading: Interpolation and map production
sections.text: Spatial interpolation estimates values at unsampled places from nearby measurements. Inverse distance weighting (IDW) gives closer points more weight. Kriging uses a fitted model of spatial autocorrelation, the tendency of nearby values to be similar. Splines fit smooth surfaces. Map production turns analysis into a readable map: choose classification (grouping values into classes), colour, symbols, scale, legend, north arrow and metadata (data about the data). A map must state its source, date and limitations.

sections.heading: Applications and limitations
sections.text: GIS supports land-use planning, health service location, transport, disaster risk, agriculture and environmental monitoring. Limitations matter. Data may be missing, old or inaccurate, and errors propagate through layers. Scale affects results. The modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP) means that changing zone boundaries can change statistical results. Cost, software skills, privacy and unequal access also constrain use. GIS output is evidence, not a decision.

keyPoints: Vector data use points, lines and polygons; raster data use grid cells.
Georeferencing gives data real coordinates, and a spatial database stores geometry, attributes and topology.
Overlay combines layers, buffers mark distance zones, and DEMs support slope and terrain analysis.
For independent raster layers, expected overlap cells = proportion A × proportion B × total cells.
Interpolation such as IDW and kriging estimates values between sample points.
GIS has limits: data error, scale, MAUP, cost and privacy.

en.title: Remote Sensing and Image Interpretation
en.short: The electromagnetic spectrum, aerial photos, satellite resolution, image interpretation, NDVI and change detection.

sections.heading: The spectrum and aerial photos
sections.text: Remote sensing measures reflected or emitted radiation without touching the ground. The electromagnetic spectrum runs from gamma rays to radio waves; most sensors use visible light (about 0.4 to 0.7 micrometres), near infrared, thermal infrared and microwaves. The atmosphere absorbs some wavelengths, so sensors work in windows that let radiation through. Aerial photography, usually from aircraft flying overlapping vertical passes, gives stereo pairs from which height can be measured.

sections.heading: Sensors and resolution
sections.text: Satellite sensors are passive (they record sunlight reflected from Earth, as Landsat and Sentinel-2 do) or active (they send their own signal, as radar and lidar do). Resolution has four meanings. Spatial resolution is the ground size of one pixel: a 10 m sensor covers 10 × 10 = 100 m² per pixel, while 30 m covers 900 m². Spectral resolution is the number and width of wavelength bands. Temporal resolution is the revisit interval. Radiometric resolution is how many brightness levels are recorded, often 8 or 12 bit.

sections.heading: Reading images
sections.text: Visual interpretation uses tone, colour, texture, pattern, shape, size, shadow and association. A dark tone with smooth texture may be water; a mottled red patch on a false-colour infrared image means healthy vegetation. For vegetation, the normalised difference vegetation index (NDVI) compares near infrared (NIR) with red: NDVI = (NIR − Red) ÷ (NIR + Red). With NIR = 0.40 and Red = 0.10, NDVI = 0.30 ÷ 0.50 = 0.60, dense vegetation. With NIR = 0.02 and Red = 0.05, NDVI = −0.03 ÷ 0.07 = −0.43, water.

sections.heading: Change and limits
sections.text: Change detection compares images of the same area from different dates, after correcting for season and sensor differences. It maps deforestation, urban growth or flood extent. Limits remain: clouds block optical images; pixels mix several land covers; a coarse pixel hides small fields; and classification needs ground truth from fieldwork. Radar sees through cloud but is harder to interpret. Remote sensing shows pattern, not cause, so combine it with field data.

keyPoints: Passive sensors record reflected sunlight; active sensors such as radar send their own signal.
Spatial, spectral, temporal and radiometric resolution describe pixel size, band number and width, revisit time and brightness levels.
NDVI = (NIR − Red) ÷ (NIR + Red); values near 0.6 suggest dense vegetation and negative values suggest water.
Visual interpretation rests on tone, texture, pattern, shape, size, shadow and association.
Change detection needs images corrected for season, atmosphere and sensor differences, plus ground truth.
Remote sensing shows pattern, not cause, and clouds, mixed pixels and coarse resolution limit what it can show.

en.title: Statistical Methods for Geography
en.short: Covers probability, sampling, tests, correlation, regression, chi-square and spatial statistics, plus software output.

sections.heading: Probability and sampling
sections.text: Probability describes how likely an outcome is. A sampling distribution is the distribution of a statistic, such as a mean, over repeated samples. Its standard deviation is the standard error. The central limit theorem says sample means tend to be normal for large n, even when the variable is not normal. This supports confidence intervals and hypothesis tests. A test compares a statistic with its null distribution. The p-value is the chance of a result at least as extreme if the null is true; it is not the chance that the null is true.

sections.heading: Tests and relationships
sections.text: Correlation measures association. Pearson r runs from −1 to +1 and measures linear association only. Regression fits y = a + bx by ordinary least squares; b = r(s_y/s_x). Check residual plots and avoid extrapolation. The chi-square test compares observed counts O with expected counts E under the null: χ² = Σ (O−E)²/E, with df = (rows−1)(columns−1). Example: 40 students, 20 urban and 20 rural; 12 urban and 8 rural use the library. Expected users in each group = 10. χ² = (12−10)²/10 + (8−10)²/10 + (8−10)²/10 + (12−10)²/10 = 1.6. With df = 1, the 5% critical value is 3.84, so fail to reject.

sections.heading: Spatial statistics and output
sections.text: Nearest neighbour analysis compares the mean distance from each point to its nearest neighbour with the expected distance for random points in area A: expected = 0.5/√(n/A). R = observed ÷ expected. R < 1 suggests clustering, R ≈ 1 randomness, R > 1 regularity. Moran’s I measures spatial autocorrelation: I = (n/S0) ΣΣ w_ij(x_i−x̄)(x_j−x̄) ÷ Σ(x_i−x̄)², where w_ij are spatial weights and S0 is their sum. I near +1 means similar values cluster; near −1 means dissimilar neighbours; near −1/(n−1) means randomness. Software output gives coefficients, standard errors, df and p-values.
