Check signs, df, residual plots and the weights matrix. A small p-value is evidence against the null, not proof of a large effect.

keyPoints: A sampling distribution is the distribution of a statistic over repeated samples; its standard deviation is the standard error.
A p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme as the observed one if the null hypothesis is true, not the probability that the null is true.
Pearson r measures linear association; regression y = a + bx has b = r(s_y/s_x).
Chi-square is χ² = Σ (O−E)²/E with df = (rows−1)(columns−1).
Nearest neighbour R = observed mean distance ÷ expected mean distance, where expected = 0.5/√(n/A); R < 1 suggests clustering.
Moran’s I = (n/S0) ΣΣ w_ij(x_i−x̄)(x_j−x̄) ÷ Σ(x_i−x̄)²; values near +1 indicate clustering of similar values, near −1/(n−1) randomness.

en.title: Research Methods and the Field Project
en.short: Research questions, literature review, sampling, design, field ethics, analysis and report writing.

sections.heading: From topic to question
sections.text:
A research question states, in one or two sentences, what you want to find out. It must be answerable with the time, data and skills you have, and it should name the place, the people and the relationship studied. "How does distance from the market affect vegetable farming near Kano?" can be answered; "Is farming good?" cannot.

A literature review is a critical summary of what others have already found. Organise it by theme, not one author after another, and end with the gap your question fills.

sections.heading: Design and sampling
sections.text:
Quantitative design measures variables and tests relationships with numbers. Qualitative design explores meanings, experiences and processes through interviews, observation or documents. Mixed methods combine the two.

Sampling is choosing whom or what to study. Probability sampling (simple random, systematic, stratified) allows generalisation, because each case has a known chance of selection. Non-probability sampling (purposive, snowball, quota) is often used when no list of the population exists, or when the aim is depth rather than generalisation. Sample size depends on how variable the data are, the precision you need and your resources; no fixed number makes a sample valid.

sections.heading: Fieldwork and ethics
sections.text:
Test your questionnaire or interview guide on a few people first; this is a pilot survey. Ethics in fieldwork means informed consent (people agree to take part after being told what the study involves), voluntary participation, confidentiality, no harm to people or places, and honest reporting.

Many universities require ethics committee approval, and some countries require research permits. Rules differ, so check your own institution’s current requirements.

sections.heading: Analysis and writing
sections.text:
Analysis means reducing data to patterns: frequencies and cross-tabulations for numbers, coding and themes for text. Triangulation checks one finding against a second source.

For example, Chidi maps waste collection points in a Nigerian town and interviews twelve residents chosen purposively. He compares the map with the interview themes and reports where they disagree. Write up in clear sections: introduction, literature, methods, results, discussion, conclusion and references. State your limitations plainly.

keyPoints: A research question must be answerable with the time, data and skills available.
A literature review is organised by theme and ends with the gap you address.
Probability sampling allows generalisation; non-probability sampling is used when there is no population list or when the aim is depth rather than generalisation.
Qualitative design explores meaning; quantitative design measures and tests with numbers.
Fieldwork ethics require informed consent, confidentiality, no harm and honest reporting.
Triangulation checks a finding against a second, independent source.

en.title: Space, Place and Landscape: Debates in Human Geography
en.short: Major debates in human geography, space, place, landscape and nature-society theory.

sections.heading: Space, place, landscape
sections.text: Space is often treated as abstract and measurable, as in positivist spatial science. Relational views, associated with Doreen Massey, treat space as produced through social relations and flows. Place is a location given meaning through experience, memory and power; Yi-Fu Tuan helped make this humanistic theme central. Landscape is both a visible scene and a way of seeing. Denis Cosgrove argued that landscape ideas can express cultural and property relations, not only aesthetics.

sections.heading: Theoretical debates
sections.text: Positivism seeks general laws and testable models, often with quantitative methods. Humanism replies that people’s meanings and agency are lost in such models. Marxism, especially in David Harvey’s work, links spatial patterns to capitalism, investment and uneven development. Feminism shows that spaces and fieldwork are gendered; Gillian Rose criticised geography’s masculine gaze. Postcolonial theory examines how colonial knowledge shaped ideas of place and other peoples. Poststructuralism stresses discourse, language and power, so categories such as development or wilderness are not neutral.

sections.heading: Nature and society
sections.text: Nature-society theory asks how far nature is physical and how far it is made meaningful by society. Environmental determinism, which explained society by climate or terrain, is rejected. Political ecology links environmental change to land tenure, markets and power. Social constructionism shows that ideas of nature vary, but it must not deny biophysical processes. Research therefore combines physical data with interviews, policy analysis and attention to unequal exposure. For example, a flood study in a coastal West African city can map rainfall and drainage, then ask who lives on low land and who can influence planning. This mixes positivist mapping with political ecology and postcolonial attention to inherited urban inequality.

keyPoints: Space can be absolute or relational; place is space made meaningful through experience and power.
Landscape is a way of seeing as well as a visible scene.
Positivism seeks law-like explanation; humanism stresses meaning and agency.
Marxist geography links spatial patterns to capitalism and uneven development.
Feminist and postcolonial geography show that knowledge and spaces are shaped by gender, colonialism and power.
Nature-society research combines biophysical evidence with political ecology and attention to unequal vulnerability.

en.title: Advanced Spatial Analysis and GIScience
en.short: Advanced spatial statistics, regression, networks, remote sensing integration, uncertainty and reproducible critical GIS.

sections.heading: Spatial statistics
sections.text:
Spatial autocorrelation measures whether nearby values resemble each other. Moran’s I summarises it: I = (n/S0) Σi Σj wij (xi − xm)(xj − xm) ÷ Σi (xi − xm)², where wij are spatial weights showing which pairs of places count as neighbours, xm is the mean and S0 is the sum of weights. Values near zero mean little autocorrelation; positive values mean clustering.

Geostatistics models continuous surfaces. The variogram plots semivariance γ(h) = 1/(2N(h)) Σ (zi − zj)² against distance h, where N(h) is the number of pairs at that distance. Example: two sites 5 km apart have zinc values 10 and 14 mg/kg. γ(5) = 0.5 × (14 − 10)² = 8 (mg/kg)². Kriging uses the fitted variogram to predict at unsampled points and to give a prediction variance.

sections.heading: Regression and networks
sections.text:
Spatial regression extends ordinary least squares when observations are dependent. A spatial lag model is y = ρWy + Xβ + ε, where W is the spatial weights matrix, ρ measures neighbour influence, Xβ are covariates and ε is error. Ignoring spatial dependence can bias estimates and standard errors. Geographically weighted regression lets β vary by location.

Network analysis treats space as nodes and edges. Shortest path finds the least-cost route; centrality ranks nodes by accessibility or flow. It is used for transport, disease spread and service catchments.

sections.heading: Remote sensing and error
sections.text: Remote sensing supplies raster data; GIS supplies vector layers and analysis. Integration needs resampling, projection matching and scale checks. Models combine these layers, but every input carries error. Uncertainty analysis propagates error through the model and tests sensitivity. Validation compares predictions with independent data, and a map without an error statement is incomplete.

sections.heading: Reproducibility and critique
sections.text: Reproducibility means another analyst can rerun the workflow and obtain the same results. It needs documented data, code, software versions and parameters. Critical GIS asks who made the data, which categories were chosen and who is excluded. It treats maps as arguments, not neutral pictures.

keyPoints: Moran’s I = (n/S0) Σi Σj wij (xi − xm)(xj − xm) ÷ Σi (xi − xm)² measures spatial autocorrelation, where xm is the mean and wij are spatial weights.
Semivariance γ(h) = 1/(2N(h)) Σ (zi − zj)² is plotted in a variogram, and kriging uses the fitted variogram to predict values and prediction variance.
A spatial lag model y = ρWy + Xβ + ε includes neighbour influence through the spatial weights matrix W.
Network analysis uses nodes and edges to find shortest paths and to rank nodes by centrality.
Remote sensing and GIS integration requires matching projections, resolution and scale, and uncertainty must be propagated and validated.
Reproducible GIS records data, code, software versions and parameters, while critical GIS examines the power in data categories and maps.

en.title: Climate Change Adaptation and Resilience
en.short: Scenarios, downscaling, vulnerability and resilience, adaptation planning, disaster risk reduction and community cases.

sections.heading: Scenarios and downscaling
sections.text: Climate scenarios are plausible futures from climate models under stated assumptions about greenhouse gases and society. The IPCC uses Representative Concentration Pathways and Shared Socioeconomic Pathways to organise them. Scenarios explore uncertainty; they do not predict. Global models have coarse grids, so downscaling adds local detail. Dynamical downscaling runs a regional model inside a global one; statistical downscaling learns links between large-scale variables and local observations. Both add uncertainty, so compare several models and report ranges.

sections.heading: Vulnerability and resilience
sections.text: Vulnerability is the propensity to be harmed. In the IPCC risk framing, risk arises from hazard, exposure and vulnerability; vulnerability combines sensitivity and adaptive capacity. A flood affects exposed households, but poor drainage and weak housing raise sensitivity, while early warnings and social networks raise adaptive capacity. Resilience is the capacity to absorb shocks, adapt and transform. It is not simply bouncing back, because returning to a fragile state can reproduce risk. Frameworks ask who is exposed, why, and which capacities can be strengthened.

sections.heading: Planning and DRR
sections.text: Adaptation planning is a cycle: assess risk, identify options, appraise, implement, monitor and revise. Disaster risk reduction (DRR) overlaps by reducing exposure and vulnerability before hazards strike. The Sendai Framework (2015-2030) urges governments to understand risk, strengthen governance, invest in resilience and build back better. Adaptation can be maladaptive if it shifts risk elsewhere or helps one group while harming another. Combine structural measures, such as drainage, with non-structural measures, such as land-use rules and insurance.

sections.heading: Community adaptation
sections.text: Community adaptation uses local knowledge and participation, but needs finance, technical support and accountable institutions. National Adaptation Plans under the UNFCCC help governments integrate adaptation into policy. Consider a hypothetical farming village in northern Nigeria. Amina’s cooperative uses seasonal forecasts, drought-tolerant seed and water harvesting, while the council protects a floodplain from building. The plan works only if women, tenants and pastoralists are included and if monitoring shows whether losses fall. Adaptation is technical and political.

keyPoints: Climate scenarios explore plausible futures; they do not predict.
Downscaling adds local detail but also uncertainty, so compare models and report ranges.
Risk arises from hazard, exposure and vulnerability; vulnerability combines sensitivity and adaptive capacity.
Resilience means absorbing, adapting and transforming, not simply returning to a fragile state.
Adaptation planning and DRR should reduce exposure and vulnerability and avoid maladaptation.
Community adaptation needs participation, finance and monitoring, and policy should include marginal groups.

en.title: Research Methods and the Geography Dissertation
en.short: Research design, literature review, mixed methods, ethics, data management, analysis, writing and publishing.

sections.heading: Design and review
sections.text:
A master’s dissertation starts with a feasible question, not a broad topic. Research design is the plan linking question, concepts, evidence and claims. State your conceptual framework, the ideas used to interpret evidence, and how you will select cases. Explain how you will judge validity (claims are well supported) and reliability (another researcher would find similar results).

A literature review maps debates, shows gaps and justifies your contribution. It is not a list of summaries. Use clear search terms and inclusion rules, and record exclusions. Check your department’s rules on review type and citation style.

sections.heading: Methods, ethics and data
sections.text:
Mixed methods combine qualitative and quantitative evidence. Triangulation means using more than one source or method to test a finding.

Fieldwork ethics require informed consent, confidentiality, no harm and honesty about your role. Positionality means reflecting on how your identity and power affect data. Get ethics approval and local permits before fieldwork; rules vary by country and institution. Case: Amina studies flood adaptation in a Nigerian town. She combines a survey, interviews and transect walks, seeks community consent, anonymises records and stores them securely.

A data management plan states what you will collect, how you will store it and who can access it. Use metadata (data about data), version control and backups. Anonymise personal data and separate identifiers. The FAIR principles ask that data be findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable.

sections.heading: Analysis, writing and publishing
sections.text:
Analysis must fit the question. Thematic analysis groups qualitative codes into themes; coding labels segments of text. Keep an audit trail and reflect on your influence.

A dissertation is an argument, not a report. Structure it around your question: introduction, review, methods, results, discussion, limitations and conclusion. Present one main claim per slide and rehearse timing.

Publishing means a journal article, chapter or conference paper. Check authorship early, avoid predatory journals and expect peer review. Check embargo and copyright rules before depositing your thesis.

keyPoints: A research design links your question, concepts, evidence and claims.
A literature review maps debates and gaps; it is not a list of summaries.
Mixed methods combine qualitative and quantitative evidence, and triangulation tests findings against more than one source.
Fieldwork needs ethics approval, informed consent, confidentiality and attention to positionality.
A data management plan covers storage, access, metadata, backups and anonymisation.
Write the dissertation as an argument and check authorship, peer review and copyright before publishing.
